title: Toronto city executives propose free tickets to World Cup Fan Fest after backlash
content:
Toronto city executives have proposed their World Cup Fan Fest is made largely free to attend following concern and backlash over fans being charged.

In Toronto’s original bid to be a host city for the World Cup, the Fan Fest at nearby Fort York and the Bentway was classified as a free event. World Cup Fan Fests are typically large-scale watch parties in World Cup host cities that allow fans to watch games live in public spaces as well as take part in other activities.

But a recent report was presented to the city’s executive committee that proposed fans charged $10 to attend the Fan Fest, drawing criticism and backlash from fans and city councillors.

On Wednesday, however, a new report was published by the executive director of the FIFA World Cup 2026 Toronto Secretariat, Sharon Bollenbach, and the City of Toronto’s Chief Procurement Officer, Geneviève Sharkey. It requested that of the 20,000 general admission tickets available each day, 15,600 will be free, pending final approval from Toronto’s City Council.

Council is expected to vote on this new measure during meetings this week.

The new report estimates that up to 20,000 people will attend the Fan Fest per day over 22 days. The city of Toronto has laid out plans for those 20,000 attendees:

·     General admission tickets available at no cost: 15,600 per day
·     Dedicated community group tickets at no cost: 500 per day
·     Premium Tickets Available for $100 to $300 (CAD): 3,900 per day

Toronto City Councillor Josh Matlow (Ward 12, Toronto-St. Paul’s) was a driving force in trying to ensure the Fan Fest remained free to all attendees. In an interview with The Athletic, Matlow laid out his concerns over the prospect of people paying to attend a Fan Fest.

“Toronto taxpayers have already paid for these games with $180 million of their tax dollars,” Matlow told The Athletic. “By hosting many visitors from around the world, there will be more traffic congestion. There will be challenges to get around their own city. And whether you think it’s worth it or not, that will be a reality.

“Torontonians are already getting a lot into these games. The average Torontonian will not be able to afford to ever go to the games when tickets go for thousands of dollars.”

Costs for World Cup tickets have ballooned. Toronto will host six World Cup games, including Canada’s opening game against Bosnia and Herzegovina on June 12.

“The whole point of the Fan Fest was to create a free and inclusive place — which was advertised as such — so that even if you can’t afford to go into Toronto Stadium and watch your team play, you can at least be in the area,” Matlow continued. “You could be at Fort York, you can be part of the scene. You can feel involved in this major global event that your city is hosting.

“And the whole point of keeping it free and inclusive, the spirit of which is that it doesn’t matter your economic means or where you’re from or who you are. That was the whole point of it.”

On Wednesday, Matlow posted on X that he confirmed with the FIFA World Cup 2026 Toronto Secretariat that “the Fan Festival, that was promised to Torontonians as a free and inclusive event, will now in fact be free for all general admission.”

Matlow said that the reason he was given by Toronto’s 2026 World Cup committee for the Fan Fest being ticketed and for fans being charged was to prevent against crowds growing beyond capacity at Fort York.

“Which I don’t think is unreasonable, but the question I still asked was: what is the causal relationship between charging a fee and crowd control?” Matlow said. “You can still manage the attendance and how many people can be at a certain place at a certain time.”
